One of the original four European 'noble hop' varieties, grown for centuries in the Žatec region of Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), it imparts the mild, spicy, earthy, floral bitterness that defines classic Czech and German pilsner beer styles, a subtle character quite different from the bold citrus and tropical fruit notes of modern American hop varieties. It is a lower-yielding, more disease-susceptible variety than many modern hybrid hops, reflecting its long, unimproved heritage, and rewards patient, attentive growing rather than the vigorous, high-output performance of newer cultivars. Train young bines up a sturdy support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and expect a lighter yield than modern high-alpha varieties in exchange for its classic, historic flavor profile.

Released in 2012, this vigorous, high-yielding American hop produces cones with an unusually complex aroma profile combining tropical fruit, citrus, pine, and berry notes all at once, living up to its name by contributing a shifting mosaic of different flavor impressions depending on how it is used in a beer recipe. Its complexity and versatility across both bittering and late-addition aromatic brewing uses have made it one of the most in-demand hop varieties among craft brewers since its release, commanding premium prices and frequently being in short supply. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture through the growing season.

Released in the early 2000s, this high-alpha dual-purpose hop delivers a distinctive combination of passionfruit and pine aromas alongside earthy, dank undertones that became a signature flavor of the West Coast IPA style, and its high alpha acid content also makes it effective as a clean bittering hop. Its unique aroma profile and versatility for both bittering and late-addition dry-hopping uses have made it a foundational variety in modern American craft brewing since its introduction, prized enough that supply is often constrained relative to brewer demand. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery and spring back when squeezed, and provide consistent moisture and full sun through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability.

directions: Plant rhizome cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun next to a tall trellis or arbor, since vines climb 15-20 feet in a season; Amarillo is a trademarked hop variety with proprietary status limiting commercial rhizome availability. Discovered as a chance seedling in Washington's Yakima Valley in the 1990s and named for its bright golden-orange color, this widely used American aroma hop delivers pronounced orange citrus and floral notes that became a defining character of American pale ale and IPA styles through the 2000s and remains a brewer favorite for its distinctive, bright citrus aromatics. Its exact genetic parentage was kept proprietary for years, and while cuttings are now more widely available to home growers, tracking down true, correctly identified Amarillo rhizomes can still be more difficult than sourcing more common commercial hop varieties. Train young bines up a sturdy tall support each spring, harvest cones in late summer once they feel dry and papery, and provide full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yabukita tea is a cold-hardy cultivar bred in Japan and tolerates more winter cold than many other tea cultivars. Developed in Shizuoka Prefecture in the early twentieth century and released commercially in 1953, this cultivar became so dominant in Japanese tea production that it now accounts for the large majority of all tea grown in Japan, prized for its balanced, clean, slightly sweet flavor well suited to sencha and other steamed green tea styles. Its relatively good cold hardiness compared to many tea cultivars, combined with reliable yields and disease resistance, made it the standard choice for Japanese tea farmers for decades and a natural benchmark against which newer Japanese tea cultivars are still compared. Harvest the youngest leaves and unopened buds by hand in spring for the highest-quality tea, and prune the shrub into a rounded hedge form typical of commercial tea cultivation to encourage dense, flush new growth.
